h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed node 1 carries no signal so edge 2 is disconnected and its gain shrinks toward zero.
With edge 0 none node 1 is empty so edge 4 passes nothing and the upgrade has no effect.
With edge 5 none node 2 cannot reach the output so edge 1 is disconnected and its gain vanishes.
Edge 2 feeds node 2 which is cut from the output when edge 5 is none, so the gain shrinks toward zero.
Adding a 3x3 conv on the direct input-output path is a large gain when it replaces an empty edge and a smaller one when it replaces an already useful op.
Replacing an already strong conv1x1 on the output edge leaves little headroom, so the upgrade gains less than when it fills an empty or weak slot.
Filling an empty edge with a 3x3 conv adds new capacity and a new path, so it gains more than swapping one op for another.
With edge 0 none node 1 is empty so a conv on edge 4 processes nothing and its gain collapses.
Edge 0 already holds a strong conv, so upgrading it to 3x3 gives a smaller gain than replacing a weak or empty op.
An empty output edge cuts off the node 2 path, so adding a 3x3 conv there reconnects it and gains more than replacing an existing op.
